cultivar: Meizhan, Fu'an, Fuding and Yunnan large-leaf
processing: A needle-shaped green tea made by hand from young early-spring buds and leaves. As with other Chinese needle greens, the leaf is fixed with heat, then shaped straight and dried.
harvest_season: Early spring, using the youngest tender shoots.
appearance_dry: Straight, neat needles, glossy green with visible down.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright yellow-green, the usual colour for a tender needle green.
appearance_wet: Plump, even young shoots of a soft bright green, as is typical of bud-heavy greens.
taste_profile: A lasting tender-leaf aroma with a fresh, brisk taste and a sweet aftertaste.

brewing.notes: General advice for tender needle greens: a glass or a porcelain gaiwan, water well off the boil, and no lid left on between steeps.

vintage_note: Specific sales practice for this tea is little documented. As is usual for Chinese spring greens, it is best bought from the current year's early harvest and drunk within about a year.
description:
Banan Yinzhen is a needle-shaped green tea from Banan district in Chongqing, a local speciality named among the well-known teas of the municipality. It is a young tea with a known maker rather than an old regional style: it was developed by the Ersheng tea factory in Banan.

The raw material is early-spring shoots, worked by hand into straight, downy needles. The factory draws on leaf grown around 700 metres in a misty mountain area, and it uses several improved cultivars, including Meizhan, Fu'an, Fuding and a Yunnan large-leaf type. That mix is a little unusual and is meant to give fat, even shoots with strong aroma.

Expect a lasting tender-leaf scent, a fresh and brisk sip and a sweet finish. Treat it like other needle greens: cool the water and do not leave the leaf stewing, or the freshness turns bitter.

This is a regional tea you are most likely to meet in Chongqing. The same factory also makes a jasmine version and a tea called Banan Zhenmei, so check the label for which one you are getting.
history:
The tea is documented as a product of the Banan Ersheng tea factory, though the year it was created is not clearly recorded. It was named a Chinese brand-name product at the Beijing international agricultural fair in 2001 and 2002, and it also took prizes at the Three Gorges Cup tea competition in Chongqing and a gold award at a Chengdu tea expo.

These honours come from the local product account, and independent detail on the tea is limited. It is listed today among Chongqing's ten famous teas in popular rankings.
